newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish crowds vent anger over ETA killing.
newsitem.headline: Spanish crowds vent anger over ETA killing.

text.p: Crowds demonstrated in the streets of Spain's major cities into the early hours on Tuesday, venting their anger and grief over the killing of a young politician by Basque separatist guerrillas.

While most of the protests were peaceful, the public backlash against the rebel group ETA led to sporadic violence overnight in the Basque country, where 29-year-old Miguel Angel Blanco was laid to rest on Monday in his hometown of Ermua.

In San Sebastian, more than a thousand anti-ETA protesters hurled eggs and rocks at offices and a bar used by the rebels' political wing, Herri Batasuna. The people inside retaliated with Molotov cocktails, police said. At least two youths were injured and one person was arrested.
More than two million people took to the streets on Monday night in Madrid, Barcelona and other regional capitals in one of the largest nationwide demonstrations in Spanish history.

King Juan Carlos, in a rare televised address to the nation, praised the Spanish people for their "condemnation of terrorism" and urged them to "continue fighting in this endless struggle for democracy, liberty and human rights".
"The death of Miguel Angel has not been in vain," the king declared from the lawn of the royal palace.

ETA guerrillas abducted Blanco, a Basque town councillor, on Thursday and threatened to execute him in 48 hours unless 500 rebel inmates were moved to prisons in the autonomous Basque region. The government refused and rebels shot him just after the deadline passed.
Blanco was found on Saturday dumped on a mountain roadside outside the Basque city of San Sebastian, his hands tied behind his back and two bullets in his brain. He died 12 hours later.

Argentine Nobel peace laureate Adolfo Perez Esquivel, who has mediated between the guerrillas and the government in the past, said he had contacted an ETA leader directly last week to plead for the life of Blanco.

"He did not give any type of assurance about the situation," Esquivel was quoted as telling Spanish news agency Europa Press. "What he told me was they were going to consider what I had requested but they could not assure me of anything."
Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar was meeting his Popular Party's national executive committee on Tuesday and was expected to discuss the killing.

In central Madrid on Monday night, Aznar led a procession of hundreds of political leaders, bearing a huge banner that read "Peace, Unity and Freedom." A sea of protesters stretching for several kilometres (miles) chanted "Murderers! Murderers!".
"They are sons of bitches, all of ETA," one man yelled.
Blanco was buried earlier on Monday in Ermua in the heart of the Basque country in a sombre ceremony that brought the country briefly to a standstill.
Millions stopped work at noon to observe 10 minutes' silence. Traffic came to a halt. Flights out of Madrid's international airport stopped.

In Ermua, where Blanco was a popular politician and an accountant by trade, tens of thousands lined the streets outside the packed chapel where Aznar and Crown Prince Felipe comforted grieving family members.

Choking back tears, Blanco's 23-year-old girlfriend, Maria del Mar Diaz, placed a pair of drumsticks atop the dark wooden casket before it was sealed inside the burial vault at the town cemetery. Blanco played drums in a local band.
Blanco's killing, ETA 10th assassination this year, has marked a turning point. Basques who once whispered their opposition to ETA in private are now screaming it in public.
In one telling moment, some members of the elite anti-ETA units of the Basque police defiantly stripped off the masks they normally wear to protect their identities and avoid retaliation.
